title: The Great Desi Grocery Expansion: How Indian Supermarkets Are Going Big-Box Across America
excerpt: From 800-square-foot corner shops to 70,000-square-foot former Stop and Shops, Indian grocery chains are scaling up and attracting customers far beyond the desi community.
body:
Walk into the new Patidar Supermarket in Bridgewater, New Jersey, and you might forget you're in an Indian grocery store. A pharmacy, a café, organic produce, mainstream American brands alongside imported Indian staples — this is a big-box operation housed in a former Buy Buy Baby, more than three times the size of the chain's original neighbourhood location ten miles away.

## Bigger Stores, Broader Ambitions

The transformation is happening across the Indian grocery landscape. Patel Brothers, the largest Indian supermarket chain in the United States with 52 locations and revenues approaching $200 million, has opened one of its biggest stores yet in Hamilton, New Jersey, and is converting a former ShopRite in Piscataway into another flagship. A new Patel Brothers location opened in Jacksonville, Florida on May 24, and a third Atlanta-area store is coming to Kennesaw, Georgia, with a $2.5 million buildout.

Meanwhile, Apna Bazar — a fast-growing chain of 22 stores in the northeast — has announced plans to expand onto Long Island and into Shrewsbury, Massachusetts, where it's converting a 70,000-square-foot former Stop & Shop. The scale is staggering: these are full-service supermarkets with café seating, upscale décor, and the kind of footprint that signals mainstream retail ambitions.

## Following the H Mart Playbook

The pattern echoes what happened with Asian supermarket chains like H Mart and 99 Ranch Market over the past fifteen years. Those chains graduated from niche ethnic grocers to destinations that draw a broad, multicultural customer base. Indian grocery retailers appear to be following the same trajectory — and the demographics support it.

Nearly 5.5 million Americans are of Indian descent, with over 700,000 concentrated in the New York metro area alone. But the new-format stores are designed to attract anyone interested in international cuisine, not just South Asian shoppers. Ready-to-eat foods, in-store eateries, and familiar mainstream products alongside specialty Indian ingredients create a crossover appeal.

The effect ripples outward. Some Central Jersey ShopRites owned by Saker ShopRites have already added freshly prepared Indian entrees — dal makhani, vegetable biryani, tandoori chicken — to their heat-and-eat sections, sitting alongside sub sandwiches and fried chicken. When mainstream grocers start stocking your cuisine's comfort food, something fundamental has shifted.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs who remember the days of driving 45 minutes to the nearest Indian store and hoping they had your preferred brand of atta or the right regional pickle, the expansion feels personal. A Patel Brothers within walking distance, stocked with everything from fresh curry leaves to Haldiram's namkeen, fundamentally changes the texture of daily life abroad.

The Patel Brothers story itself is quintessentially diaspora. Founded in 1974 by brothers Mafat and Tulsi Patel from Gujarat, the chain started as an 800-square-foot shop on Devon Avenue in Chicago. Fifty years later, it was honoured by the Cook County Board of Commissioners for its cultural impact. The petition from Indian families in State College, Pennsylvania, begging Patel Brothers to open a store in their college town speaks to how deeply these stores function as community anchors — not just shops, but gathering points for a culture maintained far from home.

## What's Next

The expansion shows no signs of slowing. Patidar is building a new-format prototype in central New Jersey. Apna Bazar is eyeing New England. And as Indian cuisine itself goes mainstream in American restaurants and packaged foods, the grocery infrastructure to support home cooking is scaling to match.

For the diaspora, these big, bright, well-stocked stores offer something beyond convenience. They're a visible marker that Indian food culture in America has graduated from the margins to the mainstream aisle — and the community that sustains it is too large, too rooted, and too hungry to ignore.
author: Diaspora Desk
